entities.summary:
Jan Latalski (1463–1540), a towering figure in the ecclesiastical and political landscape of late medieval and early modern Poland, ascended through the highest ranks of the Catholic Church to become Archbishop of Gniezno and Primate of Poland. His career, spanning the reigns of three Jagiellonian monarchs—John I Albert, Alexander Jagiellon, and Sigismund I the Old—was characterized by a blend of astute administrative skill, diplomatic engagement, and significant patronage. Latalski’s life intersected with a pivotal period of state consolidation and the nascent challenges of the Reformation, positioning him at the nexus of spiritual authority and temporal power within the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.

Latalski's ecclesiastical ascent began with his appointment as Bishop of Poznań in 1525, a crucial diocese in Greater Poland, where he focused on administrative reforms and strengthening Catholic doctrine amidst growing Protestant influences. His elevation to Bishop of Kraków in 1536 placed him in charge of the wealthiest and most politically influential diocese in the kingdom, often seen as a stepping stone to the primacy. The pinnacle of his career arrived in 1537 when he was consecrated Archbishop of Gniezno, thereby assuming the title of Primate of Poland. In this role, Latalski presided over the Polish Church, convened synods, and played a significant advisory role to King Sigismund I, particularly concerning foreign policy and dynastic matters, including the delicate relationship with the Habsburgs and the Ottoman Empire.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Jan Latalski's leadership as Primate of Poland helped stabilize the Catholic Church's position and influence within the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth during the initial challenges of the Reformation, impacting the religious trajectory of the region. His administrative and diplomatic contributions solidified the institutional power of the Church for decades to come.
